theory.intro: A **logarithmic equation** has the unknown inside a log; an **exponential equation** has it in the index. Both are solved by moving to the other form — index form for a log, logarithms for a power.
facts: $\log_{a}x=k$ means $x=a^{k}$ — the base raised to the number the log equals. A logarithm requires a positive base unequal to $1$ and a positive argument: $a>0$, $a\ne1$ and $x>0$.

$\log_{x}a=k$ means $x^{k}=a$. For $k
e0$, $x=a^{1/k}$; the base must satisfy $x>0$ and $x
e1$, and the argument must satisfy $a>0$. For $k=0$, every admissible base satisfies the equation when $a=1$; when $a
e1$, there is no solution.
A negative or fractional $k$ is valid: $\log_{a}x=-2$ gives $x=a^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{a^{2}}$.
If $a^{m}=a^{n}$ (with $a>0$, $a\ne1$) then $m=n$, so rewrite $243$ as $3^{5}$ or $\dfrac{1}{512}$ as $2^{-9}$ and read the index off.
When the sides cannot share a base, take $\log_{10}$ of both sides; $\log_{10}a^{x}=x\log_{10}a$ brings the index down.
**Change of base:** $\log_{a}b=\dfrac{\log_{10}b}{\log_{10}a}$ turns the answer into a number your calculator can find.
For $k\times a^{x}=b$, divide by $k$ to isolate $a^{x}$ **before** taking logarithms.
In a model such as $FV=PV(1+r)^{n}$, substitute, divide to isolate the power, then take logarithms to find $n$.
For a positive base $a>0$, $a^{x}=b$ with $b\le0$ has no solution, because a positive base raised to any index stays positive.
Keep the full value in the calculator and round once, to the accuracy the question asks.
steps: Rewrite a logarithmic equation in index form, or write both sides of an exponential equation to a common base if possible.
If a coefficient multiplies the power, divide to isolate the exponential term.
Take $\log_{10}$ of both sides and use $\log_{10}a^{x}=x\log_{10}a$ to bring the index down.
Make the unknown the subject and evaluate, rounding as the question asks.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Write in index form.
$\begin{align*}x^{-2}&=\dfrac{1}{25}\\\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}&=\dfrac{1}{25}\\x^{2}&=25\\x&=5\end{align*}$
The base must be positive and unequal to $1$, so $-5$ is excluded.

Write both sides as powers of $2$.
$\begin{align*}(2^{4})^{x}&=2^{3}\\2^{4x}&=2^{3}\\4x&=3\\x&=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{align*}$

Take logarithms of both sides and use the power law.
$\begin{align*}\log_{10}(2^{x})&=\log_{10}5\\x\log_{10}2&=\log_{10}5\\x&=\dfrac{\log_{10}5}{\log_{10}2}\\x&\approx2.322\end{align*}$

Divide by $4$ to isolate the power, then take logarithms.
$\begin{align*}3^{x}&=20\\\log_{10}(3^{x})&=\log_{10}20\\x\log_{10}3&=\log_{10}20\\x&=\dfrac{\log_{10}20}{\log_{10}3}\\x&\approx2.727\end{align*}$

Divide by $5$, then write both sides with the same base.
$\begin{align*}4^{x}&=64\\4^{x}&=4^{3}\\x&=3\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: An investment of $\$12\,000$ grows at $10\%$ p.a. Its value after $n$ years is $FV=12\,000(1.10)^{n}$. Find the time required to reach $\$24\,000$, correct to $2$ decimal places.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Substitute the target value, isolate the power, then take logarithms.
$\begin{align*}24\,000&=12\,000(1.10)^{n}\\2&=(1.10)^{n}\\\log_{10}2&=\log_{10}((1.10)^{n})\\\log_{10}2&=n\log_{10}(1.10)\\n&=\dfrac{\log_{10}2}{\log_{10}(1.10)}\\n&\approx7.27\end{align*}$
The investment reaches the target after approximately $7.27$ years.

development.question_text:
An investment of $\$20\,000$ grows at $6\%$ p.a., so its value after $n$ years is $FV=20\,000(1.06)^{n}$.
Find the number of years for it to reach $\$50\,000$, correct to $2$ decimal places.

mastery.question_text:
A car bought for $\$300\,000$ loses $8\%$ of its value each year, so its value after $n$ years is $S=300\,000(0.92)^{n}$.
Find how long it takes to fall to half its original value, correct to the nearest $0.1$ years.

An investment of $\$5\,000$ grows at $8\%$ p.a., so its value after $n$ years is $FV=5\,000(1.08)^{n}$.
Find how long it takes to reach $\$20\,000$, correct to the nearest $0.1$ years.
